chapter.title: Provider identity, transport, ownership and protocol checks

pitfalls.failure: A protocol peer can establish host state semantics without proving external provider behavior.
pitfalls.recovery: Keep peer authority explicit and retain external provider performance as frontier.

frontier: Finite peers prove host transport/state semantics; external provider account/model performance and real ConPTY remain outside the observed authority.
Nine Codex mapping cases and two terminal broker/PC-owner HTTP cases are covered by the separate a-sessions chapter.
guidance: Before a provider action, observe the selected device/session/folder and writer. Refuse foreign or busy writers before any resume/start/fork; a current idle app can share only the documented Claude path.

Provider adapters check their manual invariants on each real owner-boundary call: identity, options, event/pending state, bounded chronological page, media, hidden subprocess and public billing projection.
A turn completion receipt binds requested run to returned session; an expired connection generation cannot answer old requests and an in-flight action is never resent.

Self-check starts an isolated system-Python child under its supplied scratch root. Procedures launch finite protocol peers and actual hooks, parse real appended/tail transcripts, acquire a separate OS lock, and observe RPC/stream/approval/question/trust/goals/compaction/stop/crash.

Synthetic sign-in status/code/URLs are protocol data; no external provider account, credential file, model or live app is accessed. Interactive peer pipes prove hooks/transcripts/trust semantics; real ConPTY remains frontier.

Current output transparency cap is256KiB. Current terminal folder trust waits for a recognized native menu and explicit approval; delayed goal resume snapshots cannot erase pending set/clear receipts.
